title: Josiah's Covenant, Reform, and Death at Megiddo
summary: Josiah reads the Book of the Covenant to all the people, and king and people pledge themselves to keep it. He then purges Judah and the former northern kingdom of idolatry, from the temple courts to the shrine at Bethel, and celebrates a Passover unlike any since the judges. Yet the LORD's anger over Manasseh's sins does not turn away. Josiah is killed by Pharaoh Neco at Megiddo, and his sons Jehoahaz and Jehoiakim become kings under Egyptian control, both doing evil.
story: In chapter 22 the Book of the Law was found and Huldah announced both judgment on Jerusalem and mercy for Josiah. This chapter shows what the king did with the time he was given. It is the most thorough reform in the history of Israel or Judah, and it reaches back through the whole story: it removes the high places Solomon built (verse 13), destroys the altar Jeroboam set up at Bethel (verse 15), and fulfills a prophecy spoken about three centuries earlier (1 Kings 13:2). Verse 25 gives Josiah the highest praise of any king in the book. Then verses 26-27 deliver the hard word: the reform could not reverse the judgment. The chapter ends with Judah passing into the hands of foreign powers, first Egypt and then, in chapter 24, Babylon. From here the book moves quickly toward the end.
historical:
The reform began in Josiah's eighteenth year, about 622 BC. Assyria was collapsing: Nineveh fell to the Babylonians and Medes in 612 BC, and the remnant of the Assyrian government retreated to Harran in northern Mesopotamia. In 609 BC Pharaoh Neco II of Egypt marched north to support Assyria against Babylon, since Egypt preferred a weak Assyria to a strong Babylon. The Babylonian Chronicle, a series of cuneiform tablets recording events year by year, confirms an Egyptian army coming to Assyria's aid in 609. Josiah's reasons for confronting Neco at Megiddo aren't given; many historians think he sided with Babylon against Assyria, or wanted to keep Egypt from dominating the region. Second Chronicles 35:20-24 gives a fuller account of the battle.

After Josiah's death Egypt controlled Judah for a few years. Neco removed Jehoahaz (called Shallum in Jeremiah 22:11) after three months, summoned him to his headquarters at Riblah in Syria, and took him to Egypt. He installed Jehoiakim, who reigned from 609 to 598 BC and paid tribute by taxing the land. Jeremiah's book gives a vivid picture of Jehoiakim's reign, including his burning of Jeremiah's scroll (Jeremiah 36).
cultural:
The reform touched almost every kind of worship Judah had absorbed. There were articles for Baal, Asherah, and the host of heaven in the temple itself. There were idolatrous priests appointed by kings to burn incense to the sun, moon, and constellations. There were quarters for male shrine prostitutes, horses and chariots dedicated to the sun (the sun god was sometimes pictured riding a chariot across the sky), altars on the palace roof, and the high places Solomon had built for the gods of his foreign wives. Topheth, in the Valley of Ben-hinnom just south of Jerusalem, was where children were burned in sacrifice to Molech, a god whose identity is debated. Josiah desecrated these places by burning bones on them or scattering dust on graves, since contact with the dead made a place ritually unclean and unfit for worship.

The Passover (verses 21-23) commemorated Israel's deliverance from Egypt. Deuteronomy 16 required it to be kept at the one place the LORD would choose, rather than in local homes and villages, and Josiah's Passover in Jerusalem follows that pattern. The priests of Judah's high places were brought to Jerusalem but were not allowed to serve at the altar, though they shared the priests' food (verse 9), a middle position between full service and removal.
literary: The chapter has three parts. Verses 1-3 are a covenant ceremony: reading, pledge, and the people's agreement. Verses 4-24 are a long catalog of reform, told in a rapid sequence of verbs (removed, burned, tore down, desecrated, smashed, cut down, ground to powder). The catalog moves outward from the temple to Jerusalem, to Judah, to Bethel, and to the cities of Samaria, and then back to Jerusalem for the Passover. Verses 16-18, the tomb of the man of God at Bethel, pause the catalog to show prophecy fulfilled. Verse 25 is the narrator's verdict, which echoes the great command of Deuteronomy 6:5 (all your heart, soul, and strength). The word "Nevertheless" in verse 26 turns everything. The final section (verses 28-37) returns to brief regnal formulas, as though the energy of the reform has drained out of the story.

outline.t: Idolatry purged from Jerusalem and Judah
Bethel and the cities of Samaria
No king like Josiah, yet judgment stands

doctrines.note: Josiah's reform begins not with destruction but with covenant renewal: the word is read, and king and people commit themselves to it. Reform grows from a restored relationship with God, defined by his word.
Verse 25 describes Josiah turning to the LORD with all his heart, soul, and strength. His repentance is practical and costly, removing every rival to God's worship from public and private life.
Verses 26-27 teach that one generation's repentance, however sincere, did not cancel the judgment earned over generations. God's mercy to Josiah and his judgment on Jerusalem stand side by side.

words.note: Berit, covenant. The word appears five times in this chapter: the Book of the Covenant, the covenant the king makes, and the covenant the people enter. It names the binding relationship between God and Israel, with its promises and obligations. Josiah's reform is an act of covenant renewal, like those under Moses and Joshua.

Shuv, to turn or return. It is the Old Testament's main word for repentance, a turning back to God. Verse 25 says Josiah turned to the LORD with all his heart, and verse 26 uses a related phrase to say the LORD did not turn from his anger. The wordplay holds the chapter's tension: the king turned, but the judgment did not.

Hinnom, the name of the valley south of Jerusalem where Topheth stood. Because of the child sacrifice practiced there, the valley became a byword for judgment (Jeremiah 7:31-32). In later Jewish usage its name, Ge-hinnom, became Gehenna, the word Jesus used for the place of final judgment.

christ: Verse 25 describes Josiah as the king who turned to the LORD with all his heart, soul, and strength, fulfilling the great command of Deuteronomy 6:5, which Jesus called the first and greatest commandment (Matthew 22:37-38). Yet even this king could not save his people from judgment or live past Megiddo. The story leaves the reader with a question the Old Testament cannot answer on its own: if the most faithful king could not turn away God's anger, what could? The New Testament's answer is a son of David who loved God perfectly and bore judgment on behalf of his people. The Valley of Hinnom also carries forward into Jesus' teaching on Gehenna, where the defiled place of child sacrifice becomes an image of final judgment (Mark 9:43-48). The links are real but thematic; the chapter does not predict Christ directly.

hard.q: How should we read Josiah's killing of the priests of the high places in verse 20?
hard.a:
Verse 20 says that in the cities of the former northern kingdom Josiah slaughtered the priests of the high places on their altars. It is a violent act, and modern readers are right to feel its weight. Several things help place it. Deuteronomy 13 and 17 prescribed death for those who led Israel into worshiping other gods, and the text presents Josiah as enforcing the covenant law he had just read. The act also fulfilled the prophecy of 1 Kings 13:2, where a man of God said a king named Josiah would sacrifice the priests of the high places on the Bethel altar. Notably, Josiah treated the priests of Judah's high places differently (verses 8-9), bringing them to Jerusalem rather than killing them, which suggests the northern priests were regarded as priests of idolatrous cults rather than of the LORD.

Christians read such passages in light of the whole Bible. The church does not bear the sword in matters of worship; the New Testament gives the civil power no role in punishing false religion, and Jesus rebuked disciples who wanted to call down fire on a Samaritan village (Luke 9:54-55). The chapter shows how seriously the old covenant took idolatry, but it is not a model for how believers today should treat those who worship differently.

questions: Josiah's reform began with reading God's word aloud to everyone, small and great. What role does hearing Scripture together play in the renewal of a church or a life?
The reform reached from the temple to hidden rooftop altars and household gods. What would it mean to let God's word reach the private corners of your life as well as the public ones?
Josiah's faithfulness did not prevent judgment on Jerusalem or his own early death. How do you hold on to faithfulness when it does not produce the outcome you hoped for?
